back: A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb.
notes: the dog barked; when the visitors arrived.

back: A group of words without its own subject–finite verb pair, working as one unit.
notes: under the msasa tree; the tall old man; in the morning.

back: Simple: one main clause. Compound: two main clauses + co-ordinating conjunction. Complex: main clause + one or more subordinate clauses.
notes: The bus was full (simple). The bus was full, so we waited (compound). Because the bus was full, we waited (complex).

back: A main clause makes sense alone; a subordinate clause depends on a main clause and begins with a word such as when, because, who or that.
A clause that acts as a noun (subject or object), often beginning with that, what, whether, how.
notes: I know that he will pass. What she said surprised us.

back: A clause that describes a noun, beginning with who, whom, whose, which, that, where or when.
notes: The boy who won the race is my cousin.

back: A clause that tells when, where, why, how, on what condition, despite what, for what purpose or with what result.
notes: We left before the rain started.

back: A group of words punctuated as a sentence but lacking a main clause.
notes: 'Because the road was flooded.' Fix: We waited because the road was flooded.

back: Change the structure but keep the meaning, the tense logic and the order of events; follow the given words exactly.
notes: too tired to walk = so tired that they could not walk.
